report:
Yes—denosumab (Prolia) reduces vertebral fracture risk in osteoporosis, with the strongest evidence in postmenopausal women at high fracture risk.

The pivotal FREEDOM randomized placebo-controlled trial found that denosumab 60 mg subcutaneously every 6 months for 3 years reduced new radiographic vertebral fractures from 7.2% with placebo to 2.3% with denosumab—about a 68% relative risk reduction (absolute reduction ~4.9 percentage points; NNT ~20). It also reduced hip and nonvertebral fractures, though the vertebral effect was largest: https://www.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/NEJMoa0809493

The U.S. prescribing information reflects this: in postmenopausal women with osteoporosis, Prolia “reduces the incidence of vertebral, nonvertebral, and hip fractures,” and in men receiving androgen-deprivation therapy it also reduced vertebral fractures: https://www.pi.amgen.com/-/media/Project/Amgen/Repository/pi-amgen-com/prolia/prolia_isi_combined.pdf

Independent summaries concur that denosumab appears effective for vertebral and nonvertebral fracture reduction in postmenopausal osteoporosis: https://www.aafp.org/afp/2019/0501/od1

Important caveat: benefit depends on staying on schedule. Delayed doses or discontinuation without follow-on antiresorptive therapy can cause rebound bone turnover and multiple vertebral fractures, especially in people with prior vertebral fractures. So the evidence supports “yes,” but clinically it should be paired with a plan for calcium/vitamin D, monitoring, and transition therapy if stopping.
